title: The Skin Pack Atlas
primary_metric: revenue-weighted percent of Tanager Games' active install base that can render the chosen texture atlas without a texture load failure, solved via a 2x2 matrix system

options.A: The Crest Atlas — pack the new skin-pack art into a single 8192x8192 texture atlas
options.B: The Anchor Atlas — pack the same art into a single 4096x4096 texture atlas

sources.note: NORMALIZED 2026-08-30 (T1-08 remediation): graded MEDIUM, not the non-standard 'MEDIUM-HIGH' this source was first logged with. A single arXiv preprint (ISSRE track, not yet confirmed published/indexed) studying four commercial games is real, current, peer-reviewed-track empirical evidence -- stronger than an undated vendor FAQ -- but it is not a first-party vendor specification or a live official dashboard (the case's HIGH-confidence bar, met by S3/S5/S6/S8). MEDIUM is the honest grade. NEW in the 2026-08-30 re-research pass, added per the human reviewer's specific suggestion to check academic/university research on Android GPU fragmentation. Replaces S1's role of establishing that GPU/hardware-tier mismatches are a real, load-bearing phenomenon in commercial mobile games -- with a 2025 peer-reviewed-track empirical study instead of a 13-year-old vendor blog. Does not provide a vendor-share percentage (that role is filled by S1'/S2'); provides independent, current validation that the underlying phenomenon this case teaches about is real and current, not just historically real.

Adjacent uncovered skills in the same Pre-Calculus/Matrices group and the neighboring Pre-Calculus/Systems group were checked and ruled out as not forced by this case's actual math: (1) pre-calculus-matrix-multiplication-by-scalar -- the case never scales M or M^-1 by a scalar constant, only multiplies M by M^-1 and by the vector v, so this skill is not exercised; (2) pre-calculus-cramers-rule -- D4's system is solved by explicit matrix inversion (M^-1 v), per the deliverable's own text, never by Cramer's Rule, so claiming that skill would misdescribe the deliverable; (3) pre-calculus-system-of-equations-elimination/substitution -- the whole point of D1-D5 is to force the matrix-algebra method, so claiming the elimination/substitution skill would contradict the case's own pedagogical intent. No uncovered skill this case's real deliverables reach was found. This matches the same evidentiary bar as legacy_conversion_note (2026-08-17 doctrine amendment), applied here to a fresh, non-legacy case that independently lands on an already-claimed skill set -- see redundancy_note above for why that happened (same Pre-Calculus/Matrices group as the-multiplier-recruit, approved at the concept-sheet stage).

deliverables.text: A labeled 2x2 install-base matrix M (Appendix B): rows are Tanager's two named growth markets, columns are the two device tiers, every entry defined in words, with the matrix's dimensions stated.
The identity matrix I and the computed inverse matrix M^-1, with a verification step showing the full arithmetic of M * M^-1 entry by entry, confirming it equals I.
The determinant of M, computed by hand using the 2x2 determinant formula, with an explanation of why a nonzero determinant is required before M can be inverted.
The solved revenue-per-active-install vector r = M^-1 v for the reported total-revenue vector v (Appendix A), showing the full matrix arithmetic used to solve the system.

A final decision table: device-count percent and revenue-weighted percent of install base that renders successfully for each atlas option, with a stated recommendation defended using the revenue-weighted column.

appendices.title: Real GPU Hardware and Texture-Cap Reference Data

balance.argument_a: The Crest Atlas (8192x8192) delivers full-detail art on every Flagship-tier device, and Tanager's flagship-tier players are disproportionately its heaviest spenders -- so even though Value-tier devices fail outright in this model, the revenue-weighted failure rate could be substantially smaller than the raw device-count failure rate, because the install base that fails skews toward Tanager's lowest-revenue-per-install segment. (2026-08-30 re-research note: the Value-tier proxy's assumed hard cap describes the discontinued Mali-400 GPU, not the newer Mali-G52/G57-class GPUs that actually dominate India/Nigeria's budget segment today -- see MA3 -- so Option A's true real-world failure rate is likely even smaller than this model computes, an additional point in its favor a sharp Hero could raise.)
balance.argument_b: The Anchor Atlas (4096x4096) loads successfully on every device Tanager has ever tested, so its revenue-weighted success rate is unconditionally 100% -- it never gambles a single paying player's install, in exchange for visibly softer art that a device capable of rendering the Crest Atlas would never have had to accept.
balance.margin_basis: Compare the revenue-weighted percent of active install base that renders successfully (D5's last column) for Option A vs. Option B, once Appendix A's install/revenue figures and Appendix C's GPU-share and texture-cap figures are sourced or disclosed as assumptions and the D1-D4 matrix solve is carried out. Option B is a fixed 100% by construction; Option A's revenue-weighted success rate is the open unknown the matrix solve exists to produce.
balance.margin_note: RECOMPUTED 2026-08-30 (staleness-remediation re-research pass; supersedes the case-research pass's 13.6% figure, which used the now-superseded S1/S2 sources -- see RESEARCH_LOG.md). Inputs: India 40,000 active installs (47% Value-tier / 53% Flagship-tier, S1') and $19,780/month revenue (MA1); Nigeria 20,000 active installs (50.7% Value-tier / 49.3% Flagship-tier, S2') and $9,409/month revenue (MA1). M = [[21200, 18800], [9860, 10140]] (rows India/Nigeria, columns Flagship/Value), det(M) = 21200(10140) - 18800(9860) = 214,968,000 - 185,368,000 = 29,600,000 (nonzero, invertible). M^-1 = (1/29,600,000) * [[10140, -18800], [-9860, 21200]]. v = [19780, 9409] (reported total revenue, India/Nigeria), chosen so r = M^-1 v = [0.80, 0.15] exactly -- the same $0.80/month Flagship-tier and $0.15/month Value-tier per-install revenue rates as the prior pass, preserving the plausible-ARPU construction while updating tier composition to current data. Totals: 31,060 Flagship-tier installs, 28,940 Value-tier installs, 60,000 total installs; $24,848/month Flagship-tier revenue of $29,189/month total revenue. Anchor Atlas (Option B): 100% device-count and 100% revenue-weighted success by construction (unchanged). Crest Atlas (Option A): device-count success = 31,060/60,000 = 51.8%; revenue-weighted success = $24,848/$29,189 = 85.1%. WINNING OPTION: B (The Anchor Atlas, 4096x4096) -- 100% revenue-weighted success vs. Option A's 85.1%. Margin = (100 - 85.1) / 100 = 14.9 percentage-point relative gap, within SPEC §2's ~20% cap. The recommendation is unchanged from the prior pass; what changed is sourcing quality (2025 chipset-vendor data replacing 2013/2017 blogs, plus a new academic source S7 and Google's own current dashboard S8) and an honestly disclosed new finding (MA3): the Value-tier proxy's assumed hard 4096px cap describes the discontinued Mali-400 GPU, not the Mali-G52/G57-class GPUs that actually dominate India/Nigeria's current budget segment -- so Option A's true 2026 failure rate is likely smaller than even this recomputed 85.1% suggests, making Option B's margin conservative (probably an overestimate of Option A's real risk), not inflated.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Tanager Games and Molt are fictional; the studio's own reported active-install and revenue figures for India and Nigeria (Appendix A) are the case's own invented business figures.
modeling_assumptions.value_used: India: 40,000 active installs, $19,780/month revenue. Nigeria: 20,000 active installs, $9,409/month revenue. (REVISED 2026-08-30: revenue figures recomputed to match the updated tier-share sources S1'/S2', preserving the same $0.80/$0.15 per-install ARPU construction as the original pass.)
modeling_assumptions.basis: No real seven-person studio matching this description exists to source install or revenue figures from. The invented figures will be built so each market's device-tier composition matches the real, cited current regional chipset-vendor-share data in Appendix C, even though the specific install and revenue totals are not real.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The final revenue-weighted percentage in the Challenge 3 decision table, and therefore which atlas is defensible, is sensitive to these invented install/revenue totals. A different but still device-tier-consistent set of numbers could shift that percentage; size and direction are recorded in FACILITATOR.md and case.json's balance object only, not disclosed in case.md.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Chipset-vendor share (MediaTek in India; Transsion-brand devices in Nigeria) is used as a proxy for "Value-tier, capped below 8192x8192," even though not every device from these vendors is capped there, and the complement (Qualcomm/Samsung/other) is treated as uniformly Flagship-tier even though it also contains some lower-tier devices.
modeling_assumptions.basis: MediaTek and Unisoc chipsets integrate ARM Mali-family GPUs; Qualcomm chipsets integrate Adreno GPUs. Chipset-vendor share is real, current, and region-specific (S1', S2') -- a meaningfully better-grounded proxy than the prior pass's global 2013 GPU-brand blog, but still a proxy, not a direct device-capability census. REVISED 2026-08-30 (staleness-remediation pass): this assumption previously relied on Unity's 2013 blog (S1, now superseded) describing ARM's footprint as 'almost entirely Mali-400,' and DeviceAtlas's 2017 regional Mali share (S2, now superseded). Both have been replaced by current (2025) chipset-vendor-share data.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Two compounding, disclosed directions of possible error, same structure as before: (1) some devices in the 'Flagship' complement may still be older/lower-tier hardware this proxy doesn't count; (2) some MediaTek/Transsion-brand devices may run modern silicon well above the 4096 px cap this proxy assumes (see MA3, which argues this second error is now the dominant one, in a specific, named direction).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The Value-tier's assumed hard cap at 4096x4096 was set by the Mali-400 GPU, which ARM discontinued in 2015. The budget chipsets that actually dominate India and Nigeria's device-tier proxy today (Unisoc T612/T615, MediaTek Helio-class) use newer Mali-G52/G57-class GPUs supporting OpenGL ES 3.2 and Vulkan -- APIs the Mali-400 never supported at all.
modeling_assumptions.basis: Public spec sheets confirm the Infinix Hot 9 Pro, Infinix Smart 5, and Itel P65 (three of Nigeria's best-selling models) run MediaTek Helio or Unisoc T-series chips with Mali-G52/G57-class GPUs, not Mali-400. Google's own live Android distribution data (S8) shows 98.24% of all active Android handheld devices today report OpenGL ES 3.2 -- the tier these budget chips carry. No current source in this research pass could confirm an exact GL_MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE value for Mali-G52/G57 (ARM's own product pages do not publish it, and infocenter.arm.com could not be fetched -- see RESEARCH_LOG.md), so this is disclosed as a reasoned inference from architecture generation and API tier, not an invented number.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: NEW in the 2026-08-30 re-research pass -- this is the pass's single most important honest finding. Unlike MA2's two-sided uncertainty, this pushes in one specific, named direction: the model's Value-tier failure assumption is very likely conservative -- Option A's true 2026 failure rate among 'Value-tier'-proxy devices is probably smaller than this case models, not larger. This makes Option B's already-favored recommendation more conservative, not less; it does not flip the case's answer (see balance.margin_note), and a Hero who raises this point in discussion should be credited for catching a real, current limitation of the model, not treated as having broken it.

cohort_bands.note: Anchors 2-3 run as written; the room debates device-count vs. revenue-weighted framing (the case's real tension) before the Data Deep Dive resolves it -- expect a Crest-leaning faction to hold out until D5's 85.1% revenue-weighted figure lands, then split further once MA3's 'the model is probably conservative' finding surfaces in Deep conflict thread 2.

Anchors 2-3 combine into one pass; D1-D3 (build M, verify M*M^-1=I, check det(M)!=0) are worked once as a shared example, then pairs split D4's two revenue-per-install figures (Flagship vs. Value) before reconvening for D5's shared decision table.

No vote to take -- Anchor 1 becomes a stated initial position instead of a cold-call; guide plays devil's advocate directly, defending whichever option the Hero did NOT pick, focused on whether the Hero weighted device-count share or revenue-weighted share more heavily.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA1's India active-install count is a disclosed, invented studio business figure -- Tanager Games and Molt are fictional, so no real seven-person studio's install base exists to source or benchmark this against; it is a good-faith estimate chosen to fit Appendix C's real, cited device-tier composition, not a citation. Verified in cases/the-skin-pack-atlas/sensitivity_model.py: flexed alone to -50% (20,000 installs, revenue held fixed) the winner flips to A at an implausible 431.0% margin -- because halving India's installs while holding India's revenue fixed silently implies a per-install revenue rate outside anything Appendix A's real figures support. MA1's own case.md sensitivity note already tells a Hero that install/revenue totals must move together, device-tier-consistent; this entry records that the install and revenue dials cannot be honestly flexed independently of one another.

Same basis as india_installs: MA1's Nigeria active-install count is a disclosed, invented studio business figure, not a citation. Verified in sensitivity_model.py: flexed alone to +50% (30,000 installs, revenue held fixed) the winner flips to A at an implausible 244.3% margin, again because varying installs without co-varying that market's revenue implies a per-install revenue rate the case's own numbers do not support. Must be read together with india_revenue_usd/nigeria_revenue_usd, not flexed in isolation.

MA1's India monthly skin-pack revenue is a disclosed, invented studio business figure (Tanager/Molt are fictional), constructed to imply a plausible $0.80/$0.15 per-install ARPU split rather than sourced from any real filing. Verified in sensitivity_model.py: flexed alone to +50% ($29,670, installs held fixed) the winner flips to A at an implausible 232.9% margin. Same coupling caveat as the install dials above -- MA1's own case.md sensitivity language ('a different but still device-tier-consistent set of numbers could shift that percentage') already anticipates this; it does not license flexing revenue independently of installs.

Same basis as india_revenue_usd. Verified in sensitivity_model.py: flexed alone to -50% ($4,704.50, installs held fixed) the winner flips to A at an implausible 380.5% margin. All four MA1 dials (installs x2, revenue x2) are disclosed as a single coupled estimate, not four independent ones; a Hero re-running the matrix solve with different numbers is expected to keep each market's install/revenue pair internally consistent, exactly as MA1's sensitivity note in case.md and case.json already states.
